title: SOLID and Other Design Principles in Practice
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of solid and other design principles in practice and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—applying principles to real classes—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study solid and other design principles in practice with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you keep a Java codebase understandable as its responsibilities and collaborators grow. In this lesson, focus on applying principles to real classes and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A class defines state and behavior; an object is an instance. Encapsulation protects invariants by keeping mutable state private and validating updates through a small public API. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect applying principles to real classes with recognizing overengineering before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Applying principles to real classes
items.text: A class defines state and behavior; an object is an instance. Encapsulation protects invariants by keeping mutable state private and validating updates through a small public API.

items.title: Recognizing overengineering
items.text: Maintainable design makes responsibilities, contracts, and dependency direction clear. Prefer cohesive components and focused interfaces, applying patterns and SOLID principles when they solve a real problem. Apply that reasoning specifically to recognizing overengineering and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Cohesion and coupling
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

items.title: Refactoring responsibilities
items.text: Make responsibilities and contracts explicit. Prefer small cohesive types, stable interfaces, testable dependencies, and immutable value objects where they reduce accidental state changes.

items.title: Balancing abstractions with simplicity
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Separate domain decisions from input/output so logic can be tested directly. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: apply solid and other design principles in practice to a small project artifact. Record the trade-off, one verification step, and a rollback or recovery path where relevant.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one listed topic from SOLID and Other Design Principles in Practice.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.

summary: SOLID and Other Design Principles in Practice is best understood by connecting its contract to a small observable example.
Key syllabus points: Applying principles to real classes, Recognizing overengineering, Cohesion and coupling.
Use official versioned documentation and tests to confirm assumptions before relying on behavior in a larger application.
